# SK4040 — The property copies a collection it could have returned unchanged

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A property's getter is a single call that allocates a fresh copy of a collection whose own type the property already accepts, so every read walks the source and allocates again.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Performance |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | S2365 |

## Why

Property syntax reads as a field read. That is the whole of the convention and it is why callers put a property inside a loop, inside a condition and inside an interpolation without thinking about it — and why `Items.Count` followed by `Items[0]` is two copies of the collection rather than one. The cost is invisible at the call site, it is proportional to the collection, and it is paid at a frequency the declaration cannot see. ⚠ **The reported shape is narrower than "a property that copies": the copy has to be one the property could simply have skipped.** Where the source's own type already converts to the property's type by identity or by reference, the materializing call is doing nothing but copying, and removing it is an edit that keeps the signature. Where it also converts — `int[] Items => list.ToArray();` — the call is doing work the type demands, there is no edit that keeps the declared type, and a finding with no available answer is one the reader argues with instead of acting on.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
public IReadOnlyList<Entry> Items => entries.ToList();
```

Write:

```csharp
public IReadOnlyList<Entry> Items => entries; // or: public IReadOnlyList<Entry> GetItemsSnapshot() => entries.ToList();
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **A deliberate defensive copy has exactly this shape and no analysis tells the two apart.** That is not a hole to be closed later: whether a caller is meant to see later mutations is a decision about the API, held nowhere in the source. It is why the rule is a `suggestion` rather than the `warning` the proposal asked for, and why the fix carries `fixIsSafe: false` — the right answer to a deliberate copy is often to keep it and move it behind a method, whose parentheses admit the work, and that is an edit only a person can choose. ⚠ **`CA1819` is a different question, and it was probed rather than assumed.** It was measured `enabledByDefault: false, defaultSeverity: Warning` against the 10.0.400 SDK, so it is silent until a repository raises `AnalysisMode`; and it asks about the property's *type*, not about copying. It reports `int[] P => field;`, which copies nothing, and it is silent on `IReadOnlyList<T> P => xs.ToList();`, which is the whole of this concept. The two overlap on `T[] P => array.ToArray();` and say two different true things about it. ⚠ **Only a getter that is one expression.** `=> e`, `get => e` and `get { return e; }` are the same shape; a getter with a second statement is computing something and the rule has no claim on it. A cached copy — `copy ??= items.ToList()` — is not this shape and is declined by construction rather than by a filter, because the getter is then a coalescing assignment and not a materializer. ⚠ **The source must be a path of names.** `items.Where(p).ToList()` is a computed property whose operators already admit the work, and the fix would have to leave a pipeline whose type is not the property's; a rule that reported it would be reporting "this property computes", which is not a defect. ⚠ **A constructor is admitted only when its one parameter is a sequence**, so `new List<T>(items)` is a copy and `new List<T>(capacity)` is not — the discriminator is the parameter's type, because the two are spelled identically. ⚠ **Indexers are not reported.** An indexer's brackets are a call and carry no promise of cheapness; the convention this rule enforces is the property's. ⚠ The fix removes the copy and therefore hands callers the live collection: that is a change to what the property means, which is what `fixIsSafe: false` is for.
